newsitem.title: USA: Year after trial, Simpson verdict still an issue.
newsitem.headline: Year after trial, Simpson verdict still an issue.

text.p: One year to the day since O.J. Simpson was acquitted of double murder charges, prospective jurors in his civil trial Thursday voiced sharply divided opinions over his guilt or innocence.

A black man who appeared to be in his 30s told attorneys that he agreed with the verdicts in the criminal trial because police investigators "bungled" the evidence, while a Hispanic man in his 30s said he considered Simpson a guilty man who used "money and 10 good attorneys" to win his freedom.
Both men were excused by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki as biased in a case in which race played such a key role.

Last October 3, Simpson, a former football star, was found not guilty of the June 12, 1994, stabbing murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman, both of whom were white.
He is currently battling a wrongful-death lawsuit filed by the families of the murder victims.

On Wednesday, ex-detective Mark Fuhrman, who was alleged by Simpson's defence to have planted a bloody glove on Simpson's estate, was sentenced to three years' probation after pleading no-contest in a plea bargain with the California attorney-general to a perjury charge.
His plea, the equivalent of a guilty plea under California law, was an admission that he lied on the stand when he said he had not called black people "niggers" in the past 10 years.
The plea-bargain upset some civil rights groups, who held a news conference Thursday outside the Santa Monica courthouse, where Fuhrman could be subpoenaed to give testimony.

"Mark Fuhrman should have gone to jail like any other person and the fact that he is going to Idaho (where he now lives) to spend his three years sends the wrong message to black people," said Leo Terrell, of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.
Another NAACP leader, Geraldine Washington, said the plea-bargain agreement of three years' probation and a $200 fine could not even be considered a slap on the wrist.
"(It's) a mockery of justice. This creates grave chagrin for people of colour," she said, calling for an independent investigation into Fuhrman.

During the morning court session Thursday, nine potential jurors were questioned by Fujisaki and the lawyers, with five retained and four excused. Those kept for further questioning comprised three blacks, a Hispanic and a white.

So far, 75 people have been chosen for the next round of jury selection, which Fujisaki had planned to begin on Monday. But at the current pace he appears unlikely to have the pool of 100 or so potential jurors he needs by that time. Thursday was the 11th day of the selection process.

Included among those jurors accepted on Thursday were a black man who said he hoped Simpson was not responsible for the killings and who found a second trial of the same matter unfair, and a white man who thought the former star athlete and movie actor was "probably guilty."
